content: The availability of child-friendly formulations and access to essential medications for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) are critical factors in managing the disease effectively. Children who complete tuberculosis (TB) treatment generally achieve excellent outcomes. However, the majority of TB-related deaths in children occur in those who do not receive treatment. Contact evaluations, including reverse contact tracing (source patient identification), are recommended for parents and caregivers of children under five years old and for close household contacts of older children and adolescents with adult-type TB. This process involves screening for TB symptoms and conducting chest X-rays (CXR) if available. If screening is positive, further evaluation for TB disease is necessary. For close contacts of older children with negative screening results, preventive treatment (TPT) should be offered. Parents, caregivers, and teachers should be advised that children on effective TB treatment can safely resume school and social activities. Nutritional assessments are also essential for children and adolescents undergoing TB treatment, particularly for those who are malnourished due to TB or other comorbidities. Caregivers should receive guidance on appropriate diets, and nutritional supplements should be provided if needed. Children and adolescents with TB should also be assessed for HIV, and early antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated within two weeks of starting TB treatment, unless there are symptoms of TB meningitis (TBM). Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should also be provided to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with TB/HIV co-infection. Managing potential drug interactions between ART and TB medications is crucial. Social support, including educational, psychosocial, and material assistance, should be provided to children, adolescents, and their caregivers. This support helps address the stigma and financial challenges associated with TB, such as loss of income and missed school or work. Where possible, families should be included in social protection schemes to minimize these burdens. Young children with TB typically have paucibacillary disease, which carries a lower bacterial burden and poses a lower risk of transmission compared to adult-type cavitary TB. However, school-aged children and adolescents may have bacteriologically confirmed TB, sometimes with cavities visible on CXR. All children diagnosed with TB, regardless of bacteriological confirmation, should complete a full course of the appropriate TB treatment regimen. Trials of TB treatment as a diagnostic tool are discouraged. Once treatment is initiated, it should be continued until completion unless an alternative diagnosis is confirmed. For drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, treatment in children and adolescents typically includes a two-month intensive phase followed by a continuation phase of two to four months. The choice of treatment regimen depends on factors such as the prevalence of HIV and isoniazid resistance, disease severity, and the child’s age. For children aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB, a four-month treatment regimen is recommended. This recommendation is based on the SHINE trial, which demonstrated that a four-month regimen (2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, with or without ethambutol, followed by 2 months of isoniazid and rifampicin) is non-inferior to the standard six-month regimen. Adolescents aged 12 years and older may also be treated with a four-month regimen that includes isoniazid, rifapentine, pyrazinamide, and moxifloxacin (2HPZM/2HPM), which has shown similar efficacy and safety compared to the standard regimen. Children and adolescents with severe pulmonary TB should receive a six-month regimen that includes four drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) during the intensive phase. Infants under three months of age with suspected or confirmed TB should also be treated promptly with a six-month regimen, with dose adjustments as needed to account for age and potential toxicity. Children with extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) other than TB meningitis (TBM) or osteoarticular TB should be treated with a six-month regimen. For TBM, a 12-month regimen (2HRZE/10HR) or a shorter six-month intensive regimen (6HRZEto) may be used. The shorter regimen has shown favorable outcomes but may result in a higher proportion of neurological sequelae among survivors. Ethambutol, previously avoided in children under five years due to concerns about optic neuritis, is now considered safe when used at recommended doses during the intensive phase of treatment. It is particularly recommended in settings with high HIV or isoniazid resistance prevalence. Daily dosing is recommended throughout the intensive and continuation phases for all TB treatment regimens in children. Thrice-weekly dosing is not advised due to lower efficacy. Children and adolescents living with HIV and non-severe TB may be treated with a four-month regimen, depending on their degree of immunosuppression, ART status, and the presence of other opportunistic infections. Close monitoring is required, and treatment may be extended to six months if progress is insufficient. Children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) should preferably receive six months of TB treatment, even if they have non-severe TB, as SAM is considered a danger sign. Infants under three months of age and those weighing less than 3 kg should also receive six months of treatment, with dose adjustments as needed. Children and adolescents treated for TB within the past two years, who are at increased risk of treatment failure and drug resistance, should receive the standard six-month regimen. Similarly, children with severe pulmonary TB who do not meet the criteria for the four-month regimen should also receive the standard six-month treatment. In summary, TB treatment in children and adolescents should be tailored to the severity of the disease, age, and local epidemiology, with a focus on ensuring access to appropriate medications, nutritional support, and social assistance.
